content_units: Ontario Rent-Increase Check for a Pre-2019 Unit

For most Ontario rental units first occupied before   November 15, 2018  , annual rent increases are usually subject to the   provincial guideline   unless the landlord has a valid Above Guideline Increase order or another lawful exception.

In your scenario, the proposed increase to   CAD 2,050 from CAD 1,900   effective   2026-05-01   does   not look valid as stated   because the notice method and timing appear deficient, and the amount may also exceed the lawful guideline unless special approval exists.
Checkpoint   What Ontario rule generally requires   Your scenario
Unit type   Pre-Nov. 15, 2018 occupied units are usually rent-controlled     Likely covered
Increase frequency   Usually no more than   once every 12 months       Passes   if rent has not been increased since tenancy began 2023-07-01
Notice form   Landlord should usually use the proper written rent-increase notice form, typically   Form N1       Fails on current facts   because it was sent by email only
Notice period   Tenant must usually get at least   90 days' notice   before the increase takes effect     Fails  : 2026-03-10 to 2026-05-01 is about   52 days
Effective date alignment   Increase should take effect at the end of a rental period after valid notice     Not valid as proposed   because notice period is too short
Amount of increase   For rent-controlled units, increase usually cannot exceed the   annual guideline   without LTB approval     Needs confirmation  , but   7.9%   is likely above guideline
Math check   Increase = 2,050 - 1,900 =   CAD 150       CAD 150/month   increase
Percentage check   \(150 / 1,900 \approx 7.89\%\)     Likely too high   without special approval
-   Email alone is usually not enough   unless it clearly meets service rules and the proper notice form was actually served in a valid way.
-   90 days' notice was not met   for a 2026-05-01 increase.
- Even if the landlord re-serves correctly, the earliest lawful effective date would generally need to be   at least 90 days after proper notice  , tied to the rental period.
- A jump from   CAD 1,900 to CAD 2,050   is   well above what guideline increases usually allow  , unless the landlord has a lawful basis such as an approved Above Guideline Increase.
What To Do and What To Keep
Option 1: Keep paying current lawful rent   Continue paying   CAD 1,900   on time unless and until a valid increase takes effect   Best immediate protection
Option 2: Ask for proper notice in writing   Reply briefly that you received the email, but you require a lawful rent-increase notice with proper timing   Creates a clean paper trail
Option 3: Preserve all records   Save the email, lease, rent receipts, bank records, and any texts about the increase   Critical if there is later a dispute
Option 4: Check whether any AGI approval exists   If landlord claims the increase is above guideline, ask whether there is an LTB order or application number   Key issue for the 7.9% jump
-   Proof of current rent   at   CAD 1,900  :
-   The landlord's 2026-03-10 email   in full, with headers if possible
-   Any follow-up replies   you send or receive
-   Screenshots/text messages   if the landlord discusses the increase elsewhere
-   Any official notice form   later received, including envelope, email metadata, or delivery details
You can send a short neutral message like:
- I received your email dated March 10, 2026 about increasing rent to CAD 2,050 effective May 1, 2026.
- Please provide any lawful rent-increase notice in the proper form and with the required notice period.
- Until a valid increase takes effect, I will continue paying my current rent of CAD 1,900 on time.
- Result:   2026-05-01 is too early   based on the facts you gave
If the landlord serves a proper notice after March 10, 2026, the lawful effective date would generally need to be pushed later to satisfy the full notice period and rental-cycle rules.
